questions.title: What are the main differences between TypeScript and JavaScript?

rows.text: Supports static typing with optional type annotations, enabling type checking at compile time.
Dynamically typed, with type checking only at runtime
Requires compilation (transpiles to JavaScript for execution)
Interpreted directly by browsers or runtime environments like Node.js
Includes additional features like interfaces, enums, generics, and namespaces
Does not support these features natively, but can be extended with frameworks or libraries.
Catches errors during development (compile-time), reducing runtime errors
Errors are caught only during execution (runtime)
Provides enhanced tooling with features like IntelliSense, auto-completion, and refactoring.
Basic tooling is available, but lacks static analysis without external tools.

questions.title: How do you compile TS into JS ?

content.text: Use the tsc command to compile .ts files into .js.

children.code: tsc filename.ts

questions.title: How to combine multiple TS files and convert them into a single JS file ?

content.text: Using command
tsc --outfile
followed by the JavaScript filename and the multiple TypeScript files.
If the JavaScript file name is not provided then all the TypeScript files are combined in the first TypeScript file specified in the format.
Example

children.code: tsc --outfile combined.js script1.ts script2.ts script3.ts

questions.title: What are the advantages of TS ?

content.text: Cross-browser support:
TS compiles the code to JavaScript, runnable on all browsers.
Static typing:
Strongly or statically typed variables ensure type safety, catching errors during development instead of runtime.
Advanced tooling:
Features like IntelliSense and auto-completion improve developer productivity.
Scalability:
Supports classes, interfaces, generics, and namespaces making it ideal for large-scale apps.
Readability & maintainability:
Static types and OOP features lead to cleaner, more understandable code.

questions.title: List some disadvantages of using TypeScript.

content.text: Compilation Overhead:
TypeScript code must be compiled to JavaScript, adding an extra step in the development workflow.
Compatibility Issues:
Some third-party libraries may lack proper TypeScript definitions, requiring manual workarounds.

questions.title: What is the difference between TypeScript and a statically typed language?

content.text: TypeScript is optionally statically typed, which means you can tell the compiler to ignore a variable's type. We can assign any type of value to the variable using any data type. During compilation, TypeScript will not perform any error checking.

questions.title: Is TypeScript a strictly statically typed language ?

content.text: No, TypeScript is not a strictly statically typed language, it is optionally statically typed, meaning you can choose when to use strict typing.

questions.title: Which principles of Object Oriented Programming(OOP) are supported by TypeScript ?

content.text: TypeScript supports OOP principles like encapsulation, abstraction, inheritance, and polymorphism.
Abstraction
: TypeScript supports the creation of abstract classes, which serve as base classes that cannot be instantiated directly and often include unimplemented methods and properties.
Encapsulation

: TypeScript provides access modifiers (public, private, and protected) to control the visibility and accessibility of class properties and methods, ensuring only intended parts of an object or a class are exposed.
Inheritance

: TypeScript allows you to inherit properties and behaviors from a parent (base) class to a child (derived) class through the extends keyword, which enables code reusability and simplifies complex code structures.
Polymorphism
In addition TS also supports
Classes
: Classes in TypeScript serve as blueprints for creating objects that share similar properties and methods. They consist of a constructor, properties, and member functions.
Interfaces

: Interfaces are used to define the shape, structure, and contract for objects, classes, and functions, specifying properties and methods that should be implemented by classes that adopt the interface.

questions.title: What is the ‘typeof’ operator in TypeScript?

content.text: typeof operator is used to check or get the type of a particular variable.

questions.title: What is type inference in TS ?

content.text: TypeScript can infer the type of a variable when we don’t provide an explicit type. This is known as type inference.
Generally, this is done when the variables or parameters are initialized during the declaration.
Example

children.code:
let foo = "this is a string";
console.log(typeof foo);    // "string"

content.text: Here, TypeScript knows that the variable foo is a string, even though we don’t mention string as a type.

questions.title: What is meant by contextual typing?

content.text: When the TypeScript compiler uses the location (or context) of a variable to infer its type, it’s called contextual typing.

questions.title: What is type assertion in TS ?

content.text: Type assertion
in TypeScript is a way to tell the compiler, "Trust me, I know what type this value is."
It allows developers to manually override TypeScript's inferred type system and treat a value as a specific type.
2 types of syntax
as syntax

children.code:

let stringLength = (myString as string).length

console.log(stringLength);  // 16

content.text: <> syntax

questions.title: What is an unknown type, and when to use it in TypeScript?

content.text: In TypeScript, the unknown type is a special type that represents any value but is more restrictive than the any type.
Though “unknown” type allows any value to be assigned to it, you cannot perform operations on an unknown type without first asserting or narrowing it down to a more specific type.

children.code:
let foo: unknown = "Akshay";
let bar: string = foo; // Error : Type 'unknown' is not assignable to type 'string'.

content.text: You can narrow down a variable of an unknown type to something specific by doing typeof checks or comparison checks or using type guards.
Example - We can get rid of above error by

children.code:
let foo: unknown = "Omkesh";
let bar: string = foo as string;

questions.title: Is it possible to create static classes in TypeScript?

content.text: No, TypeScript does not support
static classes,
unlike some other object oriented programming languages like C#, java.

These languages need static classes because all code, i.e., data and functions, need to be inside a class and cannot exist independently. Static classes provide a way to allow these functions without associating them with any objects.
In TypeScript, you can create any data and functions as simple objects without creating a containing class. Hence TypeScript doesn’t need static classes.

questions.title: What are the differences between classes and interfaces in TS ? When will you use a class and when to use interface ?

rows.text: Only include type definitions for fields and methods
Can have public, private, or protected members
All members are public by default
Can extend one class using extends and implement multiple interfaces using implements
Can extend multiple interfaces using extends
Exists in both TypeScript and compiled JavaScript
Only exists in TypeScript; removed in JS

content.text: Use Interfaces when :
You want to define the shape, structure, and contract for how an object or a class should look, without implementing its actual functionality.
You want to enforce specific properties, methods, or their types on an object or a class.
You need a lightweight approach that only focuses on the type-checking aspect during development.
You want to describe the structure and requirements for function parameters.
Use Classes when :
You want to encapsulate methods and properties within a single entity, including providing a concrete implementation for them.
You want to use object-oriented concepts like inheritance, abstraction, and encapsulation.
You need to create instances of the class to interact with.
You want to use instance-specific state and methods based on concrete implementations.

questions.title: In what situation should you use a class and an interface?

content.text: Class
When you need to create objects with specific behaviors (methods) and state (properties).
When you require instantiation of objects
When you want to leverage object-oriented features like inheritance and encapsulation. - we need to enclose the data to hide it from outer code and prevent the direct access of this data
Interface
When you want to define an object or class without implementing it, allowing for flexibility in how that structure is realized.
When you need type-checking for function parameters or return types without adding overhead to the compiled output.
When you want to ensure that multiple classes adhere to a specific contract without dictating how they should implement it.

questions.title: What are mixins in TypeScript?

content.text: A mixin is essentially a function that takes a class as input and returns a new class with additional functionality.
So, mixins are a way to reuse functionality across multiple classes without using inheritance

Key Points About Mixins:
Combines Behaviors:
Mixins enable you to add functionality from multiple sources to a single class.
Avoids Inheritance Chains:
They reduce the need for deep inheritance hierarchies, keeping code more flexible.
Dynamic:
The base class can remain generic, and mixins dynamically enhance it.
Generic Constraints:
Mixins often use generic constraints to ensure type compatibility.
Advantages
Code Reusability:
Share behavior across unrelated classes.
Modular Design:
Break down functionality into smaller, reusable pieces.
Flexibility
: Avoid rigid inheritance structures while still reusing logic.

questions.title: What are type guards in TypeScript, and why are they useful?

content.text: Type guards
in TypeScript are runtime checks that allow you to determine the type of a variable or expression within a specific code block.
They narrow the type of a variable so you can safely access its properties or methods without encountering type errors.
Why Are Type Guards Useful?
Type Safety:
They ensure operations on a variable are valid for its type.
Error Prevention:
They help avoid runtime errors caused by type mismatches.
Improved IntelliSense:
Narrowing the type gives better suggestions in editors.
Flexibility:
Useful when working with union types,
any
, or
unknown

questions.title: What are common Type Guard Techniques ?

content.text: typeof Operator:
Used for primitive types like string, number, boolean, etc.
instanceof Operator:
Used to check if an object is an instance of a specific class.
in Operator:
Used to check if an object has a specific property.
Custom Type Predicates (is keyword):
Used to create reusable type-checking functions.
Discriminated Unions:
Works when a union type includes a shared property with literal types (discriminant).

questions.title: What is type narrowing ? Explain with examples.

content.text: Type narrowing
is the process by which TypeScript reduces or "narrows" the possible types of a variable to a more specific type based on the context, conditions, or runtime checks.
TypeScript uses type narrowing to ensure that you can safely perform operations on a variable by understanding its type within a particular block of code.

questions.title: How to debug a TypeScript file?

content.text: A TypeScript file can be debugged using the --sourcemap command that is followed by the file name. It will create a new file with the fileName.ts.map name.

questions.title: How to convert a .ts file into TypeScript Definition file?

content.text: You can change a .ts file into the definition file with the help of TypeScript compiler by using the
--declaration
command followed by the name of the .ts file.
The definition file will make the TypeScript file reusable.

questions.title: How to enforce strict null checks in TypeScript ?

content.text: TypeScript helps to avoid Null pointers by enforcing strict null checks.
You can enforce strict null checks in two ways:
providing the --strictNullChecks flag to the TypeScript (tsc) compiler
setting the strictNullChecks property to true in the tsconfig.json configuration file.

When the flag is false, TypeScript ignores null and undefined values in the code. When it is true, null and undefined have their distinct types. The compiler throws a type error if you try to use them where a concrete value is expected.
